To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the Box test is the only one that is not seriously affected by the distribution of the population variances, and (ii) the Box test, the Hartley and the Cochran test are the only ones for which the Type-I error probabilities do not exceed 0.05 when the number of treatments exceeds 5.

the Box test is the only procedure not affected by nonnormal distribution of the data, and that the Box test and the Bartlett-Kendall test have the smallest average Type-I error rates for normal data.
the Box test is the best of the four tests for all four distributions.

the problem of determining whether or not several variances are significantly different.
the problem of testing the homogeneity of several variances.

, in the case of nonhomogeneous variances, the Box test is the only one of the four tests considered that is not seriously affected by the distribution of the underlying population.

Box's test is recommended for use in the analysis of experiments where the variances may differ among treatments and where the sample variances are not normally distributed.

all of the procedures are satisfactory for testing homogeneous variances when the underlying distribution is normal.
the Box test is the most satisfactory test for specifying homogeneous subsets, followed closely by the Hartley F-max test.
, if the sample size is large, the Box test is the most reliable.

, for non-normal distributions, the Box test is a viable procedure for testing the homogeneity of variances.
